title: Governance, risk, and compliance
summary: Decide what to do when a security requirement cannot be met.
body: ## Key use case
A team needs to launch before it can meet a security requirement. I start with a short exception form so the delay, the exposure, and the person accepting it are visible.
## Workflows

I ask the team to describe what is missing, what could go wrong, and what they can do in the meantime. I assign an owner and a deadline, then send the request to someone who can accept the business risk. I set a reminder before the exception expires and put extensions through a fresh review.
## Deliverables

I keep the security requirement, the exception decision, the temporary safeguard, and the evidence of the permanent fix in one record. A shared issue tracker works if each of those fields has a clear home.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A team asks to miss a security requirement or a control check fails.
### Who owns the decision?
The business owner who can accept the risk, with Security advising on the exposure.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The engineer or team lead assigned to implement the fix.
### What verifies closure?
I check the permanent safeguard or record a newly approved, time-limited decision.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Open exceptions by risk, overdue fixes, and exceptions expiring soon.

title: Identity and access management
summary: Remove access when someone changes teams or leaves.
body: ## Key use case
I start with a real role change. If an engineer moves to Sales, their old production access should be reviewed even though their employee account stays active.
## Workflows

I use the employee directory or HR roster as the starting point. I list the former team’s permissions, ask the relevant app owners which ones are still needed, and assign removals to someone with admin access. For departures, I disable the central account and check applications that have separate accounts.
## Deliverables
I keep an app and owner list, a record of the permissions reviewed, and one task per removal. The task includes the account, permission, decision, deadline, and check that confirmed removal.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A person joins, changes role, or leaves, or an owner review is due.
### Who owns the decision?
The app or data owner decides whether access is needed. Established offboarding rules govern departing accounts.
### Who performs the follow-up?
IT or the application administrator changes the permission.
### What verifies closure?
I recheck the account and role in the source application after the change.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Orphaned accounts, privileged access awaiting review, and removals overdue by app.

title: Cloud and infrastructure security
summary: Protect a new cloud environment before it handles customer data.
body: ## Key use case
A startup can create a cloud account in minutes. I use that moment to put ownership, logging, and basic safeguards in place before anyone deploys production services.
## Workflows

I record the account’s owner and what data it will handle. I turn on central logs, restrict admin access, and check that sensitive storage starts private. I make these defaults part of the account setup and run recurring checks that flag departures from them.
## Deliverables
I keep an account inventory, a setup checklist or reusable template, and a queue of findings with owners. I preserve the evidence from the check that cleared each finding.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A new cloud account is requested or a scan detects a change from the baseline.
### Who owns the decision?
The infrastructure owner decides how to fix it. Security and the accountable business owner review exceptions.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The cloud platform team or service owner applies the change.
### What verifies closure?
I rerun the check and confirm the intended configuration directly in the cloud account.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Accounts without owners or logging, internet-facing findings, and high-risk drift past its deadline.

title: Application and product security
summary: Review a feature that lets customers export sensitive data.
body: ## Key use case

I start with a feature that changes who can see data. A customer export is a good example because the feature crosses several boundaries between the browser, the application, storage, and the person who downloads the file.
## Workflows

I ask the engineer to sketch that path. We list who can start an export, how the download is restricted, when the file expires, and how support would investigate a mistake. I turn each important concern into a design change or test before launch.
## Deliverables
I keep the sketch, the decision on each concern, the release conditions, and the test results with the feature ticket. I give the team reusable guidance for the next export feature.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A design introduces a sensitive operation or changes an existing access boundary.
### Who owns the decision?
The product and engineering owners decide whether to release, with Security reviewing unresolved risks.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The feature team changes the design and adds tests.
### What verifies closure?
I check that the agreed tests pass and confirm that required fixes are in the release.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
High-risk reviews awaiting a decision, release conditions still open, and recurring design issues.

title: Software supply chain security
summary: Ship a release built from reviewed code and approved dependencies.
body: ## Key use case
I start with a release and work backward. I want to know which code and dependencies went into it, who approved the change, and which build produced the artifact customers received.
## Workflows

I require review for changes to build settings, keep build credentials scoped to the job, and generate a component list for each release. When a dependency alert arrives, I check whether the affected component appears in a deployed release and assign a fix to the service owner.
## Deliverables
I retain the component list, build provenance, approval records, and the published artifact version. I keep the dependency fix and the deployed replacement linked to the original alert.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A dependency or build configuration changes, a release is produced, or an alert applies to a shipped component.
### Who owns the decision?
The service owner decides the remediation. A designated release owner decides whether unresolved risk can ship under an approved exception.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The service or build platform team updates the package or pipeline.
### What verifies closure?
I confirm the deployed release contains the fixed component and can be traced to the approved build.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Unreviewed build changes, affected releases without owners, and dependency fixes past due.

title: Data security and privacy engineering
summary: Verify that a customer deletion request reaches downstream systems.
body: ## Key use case
I pick one deletion request and trace where the customer’s data landed. The product database is only the beginning. Exports, analytics systems, and vendors may keep copies.
## Workflows

I confirm the request belongs to the right customer, identify which stores use the same customer identifier, and assign a task for each store. I ask the privacy owner to decide what must be retained and why, and track any delayed deletion separately.
## Deliverables
I maintain a data flow map, a system and owner list, a deletion ticket, and minimal evidence that each task completed. I avoid placing raw customer data into the evidence record.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A validated deletion request arrives or the retention period ends.
### Who owns the decision?
The privacy owner decides scope and any applicable retention exceptions with Legal when needed.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The owners of source and downstream systems perform the deletion.
### What verifies closure?
I check completion in each in-scope system and document any approved retention or backup expiry.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Requests nearing deadline, unverified downstream stores, and recurring exceptions by system.

title: Endpoint and workplace security
summary: Make sure laptops meet a baseline before accessing company apps.
body: ## Key use case
I start with a new hire’s laptop. Before granting access to sensitive apps, I need a way to tell whether the device belongs to the company, is enrolled, and meets the requirements we agreed on.
## Workflows

I enroll the device, check encryption, updates, and endpoint protection, then connect that device status to the sign-in decision. I give the user a clear remediation path when a check fails and test the recovery experience before tightening enforcement.
## Deliverables
I keep a device inventory, the baseline checks, coverage reports, and short instructions for fixing a failed device check. Any temporary bypass has an owner and expiry.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A device is enrolled, changes posture, or attempts to access an app with device requirements.
### Who owns the decision?
IT owns baseline enforcement. Security approves time-limited exceptions with the responsible business owner.
### Who performs the follow-up?
IT support and the employee bring the device back into compliance.
### What verifies closure?
I confirm device health in the management tool and confirm the user can sign in again.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Unmanaged devices, failed checks by reason, and exceptions or patches past due.

title: Vulnerability and exposure management
summary: Turn an internet-facing finding into a verified fix.
body: ## Key use case
A scanner can generate more tickets than a startup can handle. I start by finding the affected asset, who owns it, whether it is reachable, and what it protects.
## Workflows

I deduplicate repeat findings and prioritize by exposure and business impact. I assign an owner and a deadline, then ask for a clear plan such as upgrade, configuration change, or isolation. If a fix will take longer, the owner records the temporary safeguard and the risk decision.
## Deliverables
I keep one tracked finding per affected asset or common fix, a deadline, and a retest result. I use an ownership queue so the same issue does not get lost between teams.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A scan, external report, or new exposure identifies a potentially affected asset.
### Who owns the decision?
The service owner owns the fix. Security validates priority and reviews residual risk.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The team that operates the asset applies the remediation.
### What verifies closure?
I rerun the relevant check against the deployed asset and confirm the exposure is gone.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
High-risk findings without owners, overdue internet-facing issues, and reopened findings.

title: Detection, response, and threat intelligence
summary: Respond to a suspicious sign-in from alert to recovery.
body: ## Key use case

I start with a suspicious sign-in because most startups can collect identity logs before they have a full security operations team. The alert needs enough context for someone on call to decide what happened.
## Workflows

I define an alert, route it to a named responder, and give them a checklist for checking the user, session, devices, and recent activity. If escalation is needed, I identify who can contain the incident, who coordinates communications, and who verifies recovery.
## Deliverables
I keep the alert rule, the response checklist, a timeline, and tracked follow-up actions. I test the workflow with a tabletop exercise and use gaps from that exercise to update the playbook.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
An alert fires, a user reports suspicious activity, or a threat signal matches an exposed service.
### Who owns the decision?
The incident lead sets severity and response priorities, with Legal and Communications owning their decisions.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The on-call responder coordinates containment and the affected teams carry it out.
### What verifies closure?
I verify the account or service is safe to restore, then track corrective actions to completion.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Unacknowledged alerts, time to containment, repeat incident causes, and overdue corrective actions.

title: Third-party and supply chain risk
summary: Put a security review into the path of buying a vendor.
body: ## Key use case

I start where the business already works: procurement. A person who wants a new tool should answer a short set of questions when they request it, including whether it will receive customer data or connect to production.
## Workflows

I use those answers to choose the depth of review. A low-risk trial can have simple limits and an expiry. A vendor handling sensitive data needs deeper review, clear terms, and a business owner. I record who approved the decision before the vendor gets access and assign offboarding when the relationship ends.
## Deliverables
I maintain the vendor list, intake and approval records, required contract terms, and open follow-up tasks. I keep proof that access and data obligations were handled at exit.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A team requests a purchase or trial, a vendor’s access changes, or the contract ends.
### Who owns the decision?
The business owner accepts the business risk. Security and Legal advise or approve within their responsibilities.
### Who performs the follow-up?
Procurement coordinates, and IT or the app owner makes access changes.
### What verifies closure?
I confirm approval conditions are met, or verify the vendor’s access and data disposition at offboarding.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Vendors in use without approval, high-risk findings past due, and renewals arriving without reassessment.

title: AI security and governance
summary: Review an AI feature that can access customer data or take actions.
body: ## Key use case
I start by asking what the feature can read, what it can change, and whose permission it uses. A support assistant that drafts a reply and one that can send it have different review needs.
## Workflows

I record the intended use, list permitted data sources and tools, and review what should require human approval. I ask the team to test whether instructions from untrusted inputs can change its behavior, whether restricted data stays restricted, and what happens when it fails.
## Deliverables
I keep the use-case record, allowed access and actions, evaluation cases and results, launch conditions, and a monitoring plan. I define who can pause the feature if the evidence changes.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A team proposes a new AI use case or changes its model, data access, or tool permissions.
### Who owns the decision?
The product owner owns launch, with Security, Privacy, and Legal reviewing risks they own.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The AI or product engineering team changes controls, tests behavior, and adds monitoring.
### What verifies closure?
I review the agreed tests against the deployed configuration and confirm launch conditions are met.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Unreviewed AI uses, failed evaluations, changes awaiting review, and incidents involving data or actions.

title: Security architecture and engineering
summary: Give teams a reusable way to handle application secrets.
body: ## Key use case
I start with a problem every product team faces: a service needs a credential to call another system. If each team creates its own approach, rotation and ownership become difficult to verify.
## Workflows

I agree on a default design, give teams a working integration example, and pilot it with one service. I document where the credential lives, what identity can retrieve it, how access is logged, and how the team rotates it without downtime.
## Deliverables
I keep the reference design, the sample integration, a decision record, and an adoption list. I record exceptions so we can tell where the default needs work.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A service needs a credential or a team discovers an existing credential managed outside the shared pattern.
### Who owns the decision?
The security architecture owner sets the default. The service owner owns adoption and exceptions.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The platform team builds the shared pattern, and service owners integrate it.
### What verifies closure?
I verify the service uses the shared store, can rotate the credential, and produces access logs.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Services outside the standard, expired exceptions, and repeated reasons teams cannot adopt the pattern.

title: Operational technology security
summary: Give a maintenance vendor timed access to equipment.
body: ## Key use case
I start with one site or machine. I ask the site lead what it controls, when maintenance is safe, and how the team will recover if a change interrupts operations.
## Workflows

I approve a defined maintenance window and a named vendor identity. I limit the access to the equipment in scope, record the change made, and ask the site lead to verify that the equipment is operating normally before ending the window.
## Deliverables
I keep an equipment and owner list, the maintenance approval, session records where available, rollback steps, and evidence that temporary access was closed.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A maintenance request requires outside access or a change to operational equipment.
### Who owns the decision?
The site operations owner approves the window and operational risk with Security advising on access.
### Who performs the follow-up?
The site technician coordinates the change, and the access administrator creates and removes vendor access.
### What verifies closure?
I verify that access expired and the site owner confirmed normal operation.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Standing vendor access, missed maintenance checks, and equipment changes without a recorded owner.

title: Hardware and firmware security
summary: Release a firmware update devices can verify and recover from.
body: ## Key use case
I start with one device and one update. The team needs to know which devices the update applies to, how a device can verify the update came from us, and how it recovers if installation fails.
## Workflows

I record the firmware versions and affected components, require review before signing the update, and test it on a small batch. I track installation failures and test the recovery procedure before expanding the rollout.
## Deliverables
I retain the affected-device list, signing and release evidence, validation results, and the approved rollout plan. I keep the fix tied to the vulnerability or defect that prompted it.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A device defect or vulnerability requires an update, or a new version is ready to ship.
### Who owns the decision?
The hardware or firmware release owner approves rollout based on security and reliability checks.
### Who performs the follow-up?
Firmware engineers build the update, and device operations manages the rollout.
### What verifies closure?
I verify a sample of devices reports the expected version and that failure rates stay within the agreed limit.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Devices still on affected versions, rollout failures, and releases missing validation evidence.

title: Physical security
summary: Control and verify temporary access to an office or restricted room.
body: ## Key use case
I start with a visitor or contractor who needs access for a specific purpose. I confirm who is hosting them, where they need to go, and when their access should end.
## Workflows

I record the sponsor and dates, issue time-limited access, and set escort requirements for sensitive spaces. After the visit, I check that the badge expired or was returned. I give workplace staff a simple way to report a lost badge or unexpected access.
## Deliverables
I keep a visitor record, badge assignment and expiry, restricted-area approval, and any incident follow-up. I restrict access to these logs according to their business purpose.
## How I run it
### What triggers it?
A visit is requested, an employee leaves, or someone reports a lost badge.
### Who owns the decision?
The site or restricted-area owner approves access, with the host responsible for requesting it.
### Who performs the follow-up?
Workplace staff issue, collect, or revoke the badge.
### What verifies closure?
I check the access control system and confirm the badge can no longer open the relevant doors.
### What can leadership see when it breaks?
Overdue badges, access approvals without sponsors, and unusual events requiring follow-up.
